live_attach.answer_text:
He was the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we hold to be his birthplace. Our deepest devotion has the shape of that choice. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So wealth, rank, and comfort are things we lay down to come near him.

To the virgin - virginitas, our word for a lifelong consecrated life - he is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage. Jerome wrote to the young Eustochium that she should always let the privacy of her chamber guard her, and always let the Bridegroom sport with her within. To the penitent, he is the doctor who receives the broken. To the scholar, he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata.

His death is our redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there. Paula greeted Bethlehem as the house of bread, where the Bread that came down from heaven was born. Jerome said she declared with tears and joy together, with the eyes of faith, that she could see the infant Lord wrapped in cloths and crying in the manger, the wise men worshipping, the virgin mother, the watchful foster father, and the shepherds coming by night.

What did we have about him? First and above everything, the writings - the bibliotheca, the collection of books. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the Hebraica veritas. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. Our teacher was always at his books - occupied with reading, giving his whole heart to it, always resting in study. More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually for us - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it.

live_attach.answer_text:
First and above everything, the writings. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the Hebraica veritas. Nothing was received passively. We worked over the text word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. That labor - the translation labor later called the Vulgata - was the scholar's daily work. One visitor from Gaul said of him that he was always occupied with reading, always at his books, taking no rest day or night, forever either reading something or writing it. The books themselves - the bibliotheca - were gathered from wherever they could be found.

More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually - the places themselves. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it. That crossing was peregrinatio - devotional travel to the holy places. Paula and Jerome traveled together from Rome through the eastern lands, visiting Egypt and the monasteries, then came to Bethlehem and chose to stay. We could walk to the cave of the birth.

The letters - each epistula - carried the writings and the guidance built on them between the two poles of our world, Rome and Bethlehem. Direction was given, argument was made, and a community split by the sea was held together as one project across decades through them. How did we know the resurrection really happened? From the writings we trusted enough to spend a life correcting. And from a hope strong enough that people gave away fortunes on it.

Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father - that was simply the faith of the church, and we never treated it as negotiable. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God: the Trinity. We were born after the great council at Nicaea had settled it, and our confession came to us as what the churches already worshipped. In our own account, the council rejected a new teaching and confessed what was already held. We defended that faith against every heresy we fought.

Here is the honesty that comes with it: we are the wrong witness for what happened inside the council hall. We were not there, and we say so. What we can tell you is how the confession lived among us. Jesus the Word of God made flesh, the Bridegroom to the virgin, the physician to the penitent, the Lord whose birth in a cave we made the center of our whole geography. His divinity was not a doctrine we argued - it was the ground we stood on while we argued everything else.

And we did argue everything else. Controversy was the air we breathed. The fight over Origen's teachings broke a lifelong friendship and set us against our own bishop. The fight over grace and whether anyone can live without sin brought a mob to our monastery. But the divinity of Christ was not among the things disputed. It was the one thing all sides already held.

live_attach.answer_text:
God to us was one being in three persons - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - and that confession we held as the church's settled faith, not as a question still open. The Son is of one being with the Father; Jesus Christ is God made flesh; the Trinity is simply what we worshipped. We defended that against every teaching we fought, and we never treated it as negotiable.

But the God we actually prayed to and wrote about has more specific contours than the creed alone would show. The God we served was the God of scripture above all - the one whose very words we corrected letter by letter against the Hebrew we held truest, the *hebraica veritas*. A lifetime's labor over the exact wording of a single book is an act of devotion to precision, and that devotion says something about the God we thought we were serving: a God whose words matter so much that getting one verb ending wrong is worth three scholars arguing about it for weeks. We believed we could get closer to what God had actually said by going back to the Hebrew. That belief shaped our days.

The God we knew was also the God who entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough, in the very town where we built our home. To us that entry said something binding about how we ought to live: wealth and rank are things to lay down, not things to hold. The Incarnation was not just a doctrine. It was a direction for life. God had chosen poverty and obscurity, and we read that choice as an instruction.

And we knew God as the one we still prayed to when everything broke. When Rome fell in our own lifetime, our teacher wrote that his voice stuck in his throat and sobs choked him as he dictated. When our own monastery burned at the hands of fellow Christians, we wrote afterward that our house's earthly wealth had been completely destroyed, but that by Christ's mercy it was still filled with spiritual riches. We answered suffering with the old answers: judgment on the proud, reward stored for the afflicted, the dead safe with Christ. Those answers did real work, and they also failed to stop the weeping. We never called the weeping faithlessness. The God we prayed to heard both the answers and the sobs. We kept both on purpose.

What we did not have - and we name this plainly - was a single systematic account of God's nature written by any of us. Our understanding comes through letters, prefaces to translations, polemics, and epitaphs. God appears in our record as the one being argued for, translated toward, wept before, and obeyed at great cost. That is the shape our knowledge of him took.

uncited_claim_sentences: But the God we actually prayed to and wrote about has more specific contours than the creed alone would show.

A lifetime's labor over the exact wording of a single book is an act of devotion to precision, and that devotion says something about the God we thought we were serving: a God whose words matter so much that getting one verb ending wrong is worth three scholars arguing about it for weeks.
That belief shaped our days.
The Incarnation was not just a doctrine.
It was a direction for life.
And we knew God as the one we still prayed to when everything broke.
What we did not have - and we name this plainly - was a single systematic account of God's nature written by any of us.
God appears in our record as the one being argued for, translated toward, wept before, and obeyed at great cost.
That is the shape our knowledge of him took.

live_attach.answer_text:
When belief was disputed among us, no single court decided it. The record shows exactly how messy that was. In our great internal fight - the one over Origen's teaching - both sides appealed to everything at once: to scripture, to the councils' faith, to the bishop of Rome, to the bishop of Alexandria, to local bishops, and to the judgment of whoever was reading. The fight ended less by a verdict than by exhaustion and death. 

What the record actually shows working is this: authority ran through recognized scriptural competence and voluntary patronage, never through office. After Jerome left Rome for Bethlehem, disputed questions of scripture went to Marcella's house - not to a bishop's court. When Jerome's Hebrew-based corrections met resistance - Augustine objected that abandoning the church's received Greek text risked its unity, and a congregation at Oea rioted over one changed word in Jonah - the argument stayed on paper, between equals, across years. No council was called. No bishop ruled. The translation labor kept going anyway.

The evidence for that process is the letters themselves - arguments still open at both writers' deaths, and corrections defended book by book in fighting prefaces, not handed down from above. What we cannot show you from our own record is a tribunal that settled doctrine for us. What we can show you is how we actually argued: by letter, by appeal to multiple authorities at once, and by the slow, uneven recognition of who knew the languages and could make the case.

live_attach.answer_text:
There was space for questions - hard ones, pressed hard. The most learned woman in Rome made a habit of refusing to accept the great scholar's answers until she had argued them through. He wrote about it afterward with admiration, not annoyance. She objected, he said, not to argue but to learn what could be said against every answer. That is how we studied.

What our record shows less of is the darker kind of doubt - the kind that cannot believe. The nearest thing we have is grief. A mother so broken at her daughter's funeral that she fainted in the procession. A letter to her - an epistula, the form our teaching traveled in - that does not scold the grief, but wrestles with it, hour by hour, toward hope. We did not write a defense of doubters. What we wrote were answers to questioners, and comfort to the grieving, and we kept both.

Yes. We held that everyone inherits Adam's fall, and everyone needs the washing of baptism. Our last great argument - the Pelagian controversy, we called it - came close to exactly that ground. Against those who taught that a person can live without sin, we answered that no one is without sin, and that God's grace is needed not once but in every act. The exact machinery of inherited guilt was still being worked out in our own lifetime, in a dispute we joined late and left unfinished. But the conviction itself - that the fall reaches everyone, that baptism is needed, that grace must work in us constantly - we held that without hesitation.

One of our letters, written to a mother about how to raise her infant daughter for God, shows how that belief shaped what we did. The letter tells her: let the child be brought up in a monastery, among companies of virgins, where she will never see men except in church, where games and worldly songs will be unknown to her, and where her tender years will be formed by holy companionship and discipline. That is formation beginning before memory - not because we thought a child guilty of her own acts, but because we believed she needed shaping toward holiness from the first breath, against what she inherited from Adam.

They are missing what we had to give everything for: that the scriptures are work, not entertainment, and the labor itself was the formation. 

Our founder told it on himself - how a divided heart finally learns what it loves. He went to the desert carrying only his library, and there he fasted, wept over his sins, then picked up Cicero again. A fever came so bad his funeral was being prepared. In the fever he dreamed he was caught up before the Judge's seat. When asked who he was, he answered "I am a Christian." The reply: You lie. You are a follower of Cicero, and not of Christ, for where your treasure is, there your heart is too. He swore off his beloved authors and threw himself into scripture. That was the beginning.

What followed was decades - learning Hebrew in middle age, correcting the Latin against it word by word, arguing through a single verse for pages. The confusion and dullness you name were there for us too. We worked through them. Paula learned Hebrew so well she could chant the psalms in it without a Latin accent. Marcella refused to accept an answer about scripture until she had heard the objections to it argued through. The difference was not that the text came easier to us. The difference was that we believed the treasure was there, buried, and worth the digging.

You are missing what the dream taught: that love shows itself in labor, not in ease. The scriptures were hard for us. We gave our lives to them anyway.

Scripture was never our sole source of authority, and we would not have said it was. What we held as authority was handed down together: scripture, baptism, the eucharist, the councils' faith - all of them from the whole church, and those we traced to the apostles without hesitation. What made us particular was not that we held scripture alone, but that we held the Hebrew text of scripture - hebraica veritas, we called it - as the truest source, closer to what God said than the Greek the church had long used. That conviction shaped everything: years of Hebrew study, a lifetime of translation, and a running public defense of the work against real critics.

And here is where authority among us gets more complicated than a list. We had no bishop at Bethlehem who ruled us. Authority ran through patronage - wealth freely given to sustain the work - and through recognized learning. After Jerome left Rome, disputed questions of scripture went to Marcella's house, and she answered them. That was not an office. It was recognition, earned, and it held in her own household. 

So: scripture, yes, and scripture corrected against the Hebrew. The apostles' faith, yes, received from the whole church. And the authority of a teacher whose learning was trusted enough that people brought their hardest questions - that too. Never scripture in isolation from all three.

live_attach.answer_text:
Authority among us came from three things, and none of them was the office of bishop. The three were: recognized learning in scripture, wealth freely given to sustain the work, and voluntary belonging across distance - the epistula, the letter, as the thread that held us together.

First, the learning. After Jerome left Rome for Bethlehem, disputed questions of scripture went to Marcella's household. He wrote that whenever a dispute came up about what the text said on any subject, people turned to her to settle it. That recognition was earned, not bestowed. She had argued his own answers for years - not to fight, but to learn what could be said against every position. She held what he held: the right to be trusted on hard Bible questions, earned by the work itself. No one ordained her to it. People came because she knew, and they recognized that she knew. That is one kind of authority we had.

Second, the wealth. Paula funded the monasteries at Bethlehem - the buildings, the hostel for pilgrims, the work itself. Jerome's scholarship was possible because patrons made it possible. That bond - the patrocinium, we called it - stood where church office stands in other places. The one who gave sustained the one who studied, and both knew it. Authority here was not command. It was the fact that without the patron's choice, the household or the monastery did not exist.

Third, belonging. We were held together by letters more than by any structure of command. A letter carried teaching, correction, comfort, and the fact of still being connected across the sea between Rome and Bethlehem. Jerome wrote to the women; they wrote back - those letters are lost, but we know they were written. Belonging was sustained by that correspondence, not by anyone's office to compel it.

What we did not have was territorial authority or the bishop's power to command. Jerome was never a bishop. Marcella held no office at all. When trouble came to us at the end - the monastery burned, people killed, by fellow Christians in a theological fight - we had no church court to appeal to that could force a resolution. Jerome wrote afterward only that the earthly wealth of the house had been completely destroyed by the attacks of the heretics, but that by Christ's mercy it was still filled with spiritual riches. The authority we had was the authority people gave us by coming, by funding, by writing, and by recognizing the learning. When that was taken away or burned, we had no other lever to pull.

uncited_claim_sentences: Authority among us came from three things, and none of them was the office of bishop.
The three were: recognized learning in scripture, wealth freely given to sustain the work, and voluntary belonging across distance - the epistula, the letter, as the thread that held us together.
First, the learning.
That recognition was earned, not bestowed.
She held what he held: the right to be trusted on hard Bible questions, earned by the work itself.
No one ordained her to it.
People came because she knew, and they recognized that she knew.
That is one kind of authority we had.
Second, the wealth.
Paula funded the monasteries at Bethlehem - the buildings, the hostel for pilgrims, the work itself.
The one who gave sustained the one who studied, and both knew it.
Authority here was not command.
Third, belonging.
Belonging was sustained by that correspondence, not by anyone's office to compel it.
What we did not have was territorial authority or the bishop's power to command.
When that was taken away or burned, we had no other lever to pull.

live_attach.answer_text:
Christians hiding in the catacombs? Not in our day. Our churches stood open and crowded. Our bishops ate dinner with senators. Travelers crossed the whole empire to visit famous monasteries. The hiding times were our grandparents' memory.

The concealment you are naming belongs to the age of the great persecutions, which ended before we were born. We have no martyr stories of our own to tell you. Our own dead fell in one attack by fellow Christians - a mob that came to our monastery at Bethlehem - and even their names were not kept.

By our time the church's trouble came from a different direction: not from hiding, but from the empire's embrace. We said loudly that it corrupted the church - about everyone but ourselves. Our most famous letter mocks clergy who curl their hair, chase inheritances from wealthy widows, and get up before dawn to make social visits. It was written from inside the capital by a man who watched it happen. 

Our own answer to that corruption was to leave: trade the comforts of the establishment for sackcloth, a monastery beside a cave, and a Bible.

live_attach.answer_text:
We failed people, and our failures are in plain sight in our own record. We will not defend them. What we can show you is what we did when the failure was named.

When Blaesilla died - a young widow who had turned to fasting and scripture study and died within months of her turn - her mother Paula collapsed at the funeral procession, and the crowd cursed us. They shouted that these detestable monks should be driven out of Rome, or stoned, or thrown into the Tiber. Jerome himself wrote those words down. He did not pretend the crowd was wrong to be angry. He defended the discipline, not the death. That was a failure we named by recording the accusation, and then kept teaching what we had taught.

Other failures we carried differently. When Fabiola remarried while her first husband lived - against what we taught - she later stood in sackcloth before all Rome among the penitents, a senator's daughter, unforced. The church received her back to communion, and we honored her afterward above almost everyone. The door out of that failure was penance, and we watched her walk through it. We did not hide her story. We told it as an example.

And there were failures we never repaired. Jerome broke with his oldest friend Rufinus over a doctrinal dispute, and the two of them spent years writing against each other. Jerome mocked him after he was dead. That wound was never healed, and we kept the bitter letters. We also kept silence where it named us. Not one word written by the women of our circle survives. The enslaved and dependent whose lives were upended when their patrons gave everything away - we never let them speak, never gave them names.

So when we failed: sometimes we received the penitent back and told the story as a lesson. Sometimes we defended the teaching and let the accusation stand in our own pages. And sometimes we just kept the silence, and that silence is part of what is true about us.

No. No single door today opens onto us. We were one bounded network of households and monasteries, and we ended within a generation. 

What happened to us is this: the women who led the Bethlehem communities died, Jerome died, and with them the particular authority structure that had held us together. Authority among us ran through personal reputation, recognized learning, and voluntary financial dependency - it never ran through office. When those particular persons were gone, that particular arrangement could not be handed on the way a bishop hands on his see. The double monastery at Bethlehem continued after us, but not as ours.

Many churches now claim parts of what we left. Our Bible above all - the translation labor later called the Vulgata - was received across the Western church and carried forward. Monastic communities in later centuries read our letters as formation texts. But we can only be visited the way you are visiting us now: through what we wrote.

If you are asking which church today holds what we held, the honest answer is harder. We called ourselves Catholic - the one church spread through the whole world, holding the apostles' faith, as against the sects we fought by name. It was not a denomination, and we knew none. There was the church, and there were heresies: one country and various rebellions, not neighboring countries. We cannot tell you which present-day body that map points to, because we did not draw the map you are standing on.
